Background

Generalised Pareto Distribution

The Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD) is a flexible family of continuous probability distributions that arises naturally in extreme value theory, particularly for modelling the distribution of excesses over a threshold. It is parametrised by a shape parameter \(\xi \in \mathbb{R}\), a scale parameter \(\sigma > 0\), and a location parameter \(u \in \mathbb{R}\). Its cumulative distribution function (CDF) is given by

\[ F(x;\,\sigma,\xi, u) = \begin{cases} 1 - \left(1 + \dfrac{\xi (x-u)}{\sigma}\right)_+^{-1/\xi}, & \xi \neq 0, \, x \geq u; \; \\[1.2em] 1 - \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{x-u}{\sigma}\right), & \xi = 0, \, x \geq u; \end{cases} \tag{1}\]

where \(x_+ = \max(x,0)\) and its probability density function (PDF) is

\[ f(x;\sigma,\xi,u) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{\sigma}\left(1 + \dfrac{\xi (x-u)}{\sigma}\right)_+^{-1/\xi - 1}, & \xi \neq 0, \\[1.2em] \dfrac{1}{\sigma}\exp\!\left(-\dfrac{x-u}{\sigma}\right), & \xi = 0, \end{cases} \tag{2}\]

defined on the same support as the CDF. The GPD encompasses a variety of tail behaviours:

  • when \(\xi > 0\) the GPD has heavy, slowly decaying tails,
  • in limiting case when \(\xi \rightarrow 0\) the GPD reduces to an exponential distribution;
  • when \(\xi < 0\) the GPD has light, quickly decaying tails with a finite upper endpoint of \(x^+ = u - \sigma / \xi\).

Probability Integral Transform

The probability integral transform states that if a random variable \(X\) has a continuous cumulative distribution function \(F_X(x)\), then the transformed variable \(A = F_X(X)\) follows a uniform distribution on \([0,1]\). Conversely, if \(F\) is an invertible function then \(Y = F^{-1}_X(A)\) has the same distribution as \(X\).

Question 1

Derive an expression for the inverse cumulative distribution function (also known as the quantile function) \(F^{-1}_X: [0,1] \rightarrow [u, x^+]\) of \(X \sim \text{GPD}(u, \sigma, \xi)\). Your answer should refer to at least one equation given in the background material.

Solution_Q1

The inverse \(F^{-1}\) of the CDF of the pareto distribution is the function that maps \((0,1]\rightarrow[u,x^+]\) such that \(F(F^{-1})(x) = x\). This function is traditionally found by switching the x and y variables in the function we’re looking to invert, and then by isolating the variables and solving for y. Often in math, it’s helpful to break down this into two cases, one where \(\xi=0\), so essentially the exponential distribution.

Equation 1 tells us the CDF for \(\xi=0\), so let us start by switching the variables.

\[ x = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{y-u}{\sigma}\right) \] Next, we follow through with isolating the y variable in the following steps.

  1. Isolate the exponential expression.

\[ \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{y-u}{\sigma}\right) = 1-x \]

  1. Take the natural log of both sides and simplify.

\[ \dfrac{y-u}{\sigma} = -\ln(1-x) \]

  1. Solve for y to get \[ F^{-1} = u -\sigma\ln(1-x)\]

Now, let’s do the same with the case where \(\xi\neq0\), again starting from Equation 1 and switching the variables.

\[ x = 1 - \left(1 + \dfrac{\xi (y-u)}{\sigma}\right)^{-1/\xi} \]

  1. Isolating the exponent term

\[ \left(1 + \dfrac{\xi (y-u)}{\sigma}\right)^{-1/\xi} = 1-x \]

  1. Raising both sides to the \(-\xi\) and re-arranging

\[\dfrac{\xi (y-u)}{\sigma} = (1-x)^\frac{-1}{\xi}-1 \]

And finally, \[y = \dfrac{\sigma}{\xi}\left((1-x)^{-\xi}-1\right) + u\]

So,

\[ F^{-1}(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\sigma}{\xi}\left((1-x)^{-\xi}-1\right) + u, & \xi\neq0,\, x\in[0,1) \\[1.2em] u -\sigma\ln(1-x), & \xi=0, \, x\in[0,1) \end{cases} \]

Solution_Q2

Part A

The standard R quantile functions take in the distribution parameters, a probability \(p\), and then compute X such that \(P(X\leq X) = p\)

#' Quantile function for the Generalized Pareto Distribution
#'
#' @param p - probability value 
#' @param mu - threshold of the pareto distribution
#' @param sigma - scale parameter, must be >0
#' @param xi - shape parameter; affects the shape of the curve. At xi=0 the function evaluates the quantile of the exponential function. 
#' @param lower.tail - Default set to TRUE, calculating P(X<=x). When FALSE evaluates P(x>X). So if p = .95, setting this to FALSE calculates P(x>X) = 0.95, so the 5th percentile
#' @param log.p - Default set to FALSE. If inputted p is actually a log probabilty, then set to true and the function will evaluate the quantile for p<- exp(p)
#'
#' @returns X s.t. P(X<=X) = p 
#'
#' @examples
#' ## Using "log = TRUE" evaluates P(X<=x) = exp(-2) for the distribution)
#'   qgpd(-2,1,1,0,log.p = TRUE)
#'   
#'#' ## Using "lower.tail=FALSE" evaluates P(X>x) = 0.4, so the 60th quantile. 
#'   qgpd(0.4,1,1,0,lower.tail=FALSE)
#'   


qgpd<-function(p, mu,sigma,xi,lower.tail=TRUE,log.p=FALSE) {
  stopifnot(sigma>0)
  stopifnot(typeof(lower.tail)=="logical")
  stopifnot(typeof(log.p)=="logical")
  
  if (log.p== TRUE) {
    p<-exp(p)
  }
 if (lower.tail==FALSE) {
    p = 1-p
 }
  stopifnot(p >= 0)
  stopifnot(p <= 1)
  
  if (xi == 0) {
    return(mu-sigma*log((1-p),exp(1))) }
  else 
    return((sigma/xi)*((1-p)**(-1*xi) - 1) + mu)
}

Part B

qgpd(0.75,mu = 1.5,sigma =2, xi=-0.4)
qgpd(0.99,mu = 1.5,sigma =2, xi=-0.4)

Question 3

Within a single figure, construct a series of quantile-quantile plots to identify which datasets are inconsistent with their stated distributions. You should both justify your conclusions and describe your level of confidence in your findings.

Solution_Q3

The provided data has variates and parameters across six different sets. We’ve learned that some of our parameter data might be wrong, so a tool we have to see which sample variates seem appropriate given the parameters, we can use a Q-Q plot to compare (1) theoretical quantile values given the potentially incorrect parameters to (2) the quantiles in the observed data. The best evidence that the parameters are correct for any given set would be if the plot of (theoretical, observed) across the quantiles follows the line y=x.

Observing Figure 1, we can see the relevant Q-Q plots across the sets. Based on a cursory analysis, Set A’s (Figure 1 (a)) theoretical values mirror the observed until around the 70th percentile, then we see that the observed values were slightly higher than the theoretical formula would indicate. I have a moderate level of confidence that Set A is drawn from the parameters provided. Set B (Figure 1 (b)) closely follows the y=x line, so the parameters seem correct. The same seems to be true for Set C (Figure 1 (c)). I have relatively high confidence that Sets B and C are drawn from the parameters provided. Sets D and E don’t follow the theoretical distribution even remotely, so I’m reasonably confident that these parameters are wrong,as seen in Figure 1 (d) and Figure 1 (e). Finally, Set F seems to follow the y=x line, although there seem to be some large outliers in the observed values (Figure 1 (f)). I’m somewhat confident that these values are drawn from the distribution, but more analysis is needed here. It’s possible that the tail needs to have a slower decline implying a larger \(\xi\) value.

Question 4

For this question, all R code should be displayed only within the appendix, not in the main report.

A hydrologist is interested in understanding the river flow at a location that is historically prone to flooding. There is a river flow gauge nearby which measures river flow in units of cubic meters per second (\(\text{m}^3/\text{s}\) or cumecs). Based on her knowledge of other rivers, the hydrologist proposes that for this river gauge:

  • the distribution of river flow values is constant over time
  • for river flows exceeding 75 cumecs, it is appropriate to model these data as independent and identically distributed GPD(\(\sigma =29.7\), \(\xi=0.62\), \(u = 0\)).

Use riverflow_2015-2024.csv to conduct an exploratory investigation of whether these proposals are valid for the dataset provided. Summarise your findings in 250-350 words, supporting these with a collection of 4 visualisations/figures.

Solution_Q4

The hydrologist has made 2 proposals, namely (1) that the distribution of flows is constant over time, and (2) that flows above 75 are distributed according to the GPD with the provided parameters. I want to use two plots to preliminarily evaluate both of these proposals.

For (1) I’ll just take a look at all of the events in the data set as a time-series alongside the baseline means to see from a high level if things look different over the 10 years of data. This is meant to be a first look across the data set to inform the later plots. Intuition would tell me that with changing climates, it’s reasonable for the distribution of flows to change over time. Figure 2 shows that the proposal may indeed be correct. The daily flows seem to remain in the same general band, and the baseline means seem to have the same general yearly pattern, probably peaking due to rainfall or snow-melt in one season and gradually declining until the next year.

However, the data is highly overlapping in the plot, so I wanted to look a bit closer at the data. Figure 3 looks at each year’s distribution of flows and provides a distribution of the medians and IQR values for the yearly flows and compares across years in the data set. Here we actually see that river flow has been increasing slowly over the past decade, with the median daily flow in 2024 being ~4 cumecs higher than that of 2015. Based on this, I don’t believe this preliminary analysis supports proposal #1; rather the distribution of flows seems to be changing over time.

Switching gears to the second part of the proposal, my first instinct is to make a histogram of the daily flow observations above seventy-five cumecs in order to see if the shape of the curve follows the shape of the GPD. Figure 4 shows that the underlying bars do seem to follow the shape of a pareto distribution from first glance based on our analysis in previous exercises. But to be sure, I overlaid a set of points following the theoretical density function for a GPD function with the provided parameters. Figure 4 shows that the observed excess flows closely follow the theoretical density function.

To be less eye-balling with the data, we can use a final visualization drawn from previous exercises, namely the Q-Q plot. Figure 5 plots the quantiles of the theoretical distribution with the proposed parameters against the quantiles of the measured excess flows. These closely follow the line y=x, providing more evidence that the hydrologist’s proposed parameters seem correct.

So, a preliminary look at the data suggests that part 1 of the proposal may not be true, and part 2 of the proposal seems to hold. However, we’d need to do more analysis to be sure.

Solution_Q5

I approached this question as a preliminary exercise in sense checking the hydrologist’s proposals. This might be for a team member or manager as a quick answer to “how does the proposal look”, but it’s not a final analysis or recommendation I might offer as the role of an “auditor”.

As such, my visualizations were much more for personal exploration and building my own conviction of what the answers might be about the proposal. If I were to present this in a more formal setting, I’d make some changes:

  1. I’d explore some more visualizations, as I could have conducted a much more thorough analysis. For instance, I could have overlaid several more distributions with different parameters on Figure 4, or even used a fitting algorithm to find the parameters which actually best match the observed data. On part 1 of the proposal, I could have conducted and plotted some t-tests to show and quantify how different the flows look across years, improving my more directional “the medians are increasing”.

  2. I’d do more rigorous visualization, for example with the treatment and visualization of outliers. Figure 2 is not complete. There are several outliers that drive up the y-axis limits and make it much more difficult to view a majority of the samples. If I were to present this chart, I might choose to exclude outliers, or better yet to choose a different scale (e.g., log(Flows)) to more clearly visualize the trends.

  3. I’d further clean up my presentation. I did not know how to represent the histogram boxes in the legend for Figure 4, so I instead opted to use a square to represent the sampled values. I’m not sure if there’s a better way to do this, but a more formal presentation would demand a closer attention to my visual presentation.

  4. I’d put in more effort to make my visualizations accessible. None of my visualizations require distinguishing between classes, but Figure 2 uses colors that some readers might find difficult to distinguish, particularly the baseline mean line vs. the flow points. For an external-facing analysis, I would put in much more effort to ensure that people with various abilities were able to engage with my visualizations.

#' Quantile function for the Generalized Pareto Distribution
#'
#' @param p - probability value 
#' @param mu - threshold of the pareto distribution
#' @param sigma - scale parameter, must be >0
#' @param xi - shape parameter; affects the shape of the curve. At xi=0 the function evaluates the quantile of the exponential function. 
#' @param lower.tail - Default set to TRUE, calculating P(X<=x). When FALSE evaluates P(x>X). So if p = .95, setting this to FALSE calculates P(x>X) = 0.95, so the 5th percentile
#' @param log.p - Default set to FALSE. If inputted p is actually a log probabilty, then set to true and the function will evaluate the quantile for p<- exp(p)
#'
#' @returns X s.t. P(X<=X) = p 
#'
#' @examples
#' ## Using "log = TRUE" evaluates P(X<=x) = exp(-2) for the distribution)
#'   qgpd(-2,1,1,0,log.p = TRUE)
#'   
#'#' ## Using "lower.tail=FALSE" evaluates P(X>x) = 0.4, so the 60th quantile. 
#'   qgpd(0.4,1,1,0,lower.tail=FALSE)
#'   


qgpd<-function(p, mu,sigma,xi,lower.tail=TRUE,log.p=FALSE) {
  stopifnot(sigma>0)
  stopifnot(typeof(lower.tail)=="logical")
  stopifnot(typeof(log.p)=="logical")
  
  if (log.p== TRUE) {
    p<-exp(p)
  }
 if (lower.tail==FALSE) {
    p = 1-p
 }
  stopifnot(p >= 0)
  stopifnot(p <= 1)
  
  if (xi == 0) {
    return(mu-sigma*log((1-p),exp(1))) }
  else 
    return((sigma/xi)*((1-p)**(-1*xi) - 1) + mu)
}

qgpd(0.5,mu = 1.5,sigma =2, xi=-0.4)
qgpd(0.75,mu = 1.5,sigma =2, xi=-0.4)
qgpd(0.99,mu = 1.5,sigma =2, xi=-0.4)


gpd_samples<-read.csv("gpd_samples.csv")
gpd_params<- read.csv("gpd_parameters.csv")
granularity = 50
sets<-c("a","b","c","d","e","f")

for (i in 1:length(sets)) {
  x = seq(0,1-1/granularity,by = 1/granularity)
  u<- gpd_params[gpd_params$id==sets[i],]$u
  sigma<- gpd_params[gpd_params$id==sets[i],]$sigma
  xi<- gpd_params[gpd_params$id==sets[i],]$xi

  theoretical<-qgpd(x,u,sigma,xi)
  variates<-gpd_samples[gpd_samples$set_id==sets[i],]$value
  quantiles<-quantile(variates,x)

  plot(theoretical,quantiles,xlab = "Theoretical values", ylab = "Observed variates", pch = 16, cex.axis = 1.4, cex.lab = 1.4,abline(a=0,b=1))
  }

gpd_density<- function(x,mu,sigma,xi) {
  return((1/sigma)*(1 + xi*(x-mu)/sigma)**(-1/xi-1))
  
}

excess_events<-river_flow[river_flow$flow>=75,]
hist(excess_events$flow-75,breaks = 100, freq=FALSE, xlab = "Flow above 75 cumecs", main = "")

points(x,gpd_density(x,0,29.7,0.62), pch=16)
legend("topright",legend = c("Theoretical density","Actual density"), bty = "n",pch = c(16,22))
